claims.text: cleanup_worktree runs a recursive delete, unattended, in a finally: block (see daedalus.spine.attempt), against a directory that CANDIDATE CODE HAS BEEN WRITING TO.
claims.why: cleanup_worktree is not defined in this chunk; the claim about its call site in daedalus.spine.attempt is outside this chunk.

claims.text: A cleanup target is deleted only if the manager can prove it is the thing the manager itself allocated. Anything unproven raises WorktreeContainmentError and nothing is removed.
claims.why: The deletion logic and the proof are in cleanup_worktree and _remove_tree_no_follow, which are not in this chunk.

claims.text: The concrete attack this defends against: candidate code deletes its own worktree directory and replaces it with a symlink -- or, on Windows, a directory junction (mklink /J), which os.path.islink DOES NOT SEE -- aimed at the developer's primary checkout.
claims.why: The claim that os.path.islink does not see junctions is supported by _is_reparse_point's docstring and code, which checks FILE_ATTRIBUTE_REPARSE_POINT and st_reparse_tag in addition to S_ISLNK and islink.

claims.text: Path.resolve() before the safety check turns the link into its target, so the subsequent delete is handed a real directory (the primary checkout) and never sees a link at all. This is why nothing here resolves before it checks: check no-follow first, then operate on the unresolved path.
claims.why: The code consistently uses lstat and lexical operations; _lexical explicitly avoids resolve() and _is_reparse_point and _path_identity use lstat. The claim that resolve() follows links is consistent with Python semantics.

claims.text: git worktree remove --force performs its own recursive delete and FOLLOWS a junction planted inside the worktree (measured: exit 0, empty stderr, target contents gone). So git's removal is not used at all any more.
claims.why: This chunk does not contain the removal code; it only mentions that git's removal is not used. The measured behavior is not verifiable here.

claims.text: shutil.rmtree is NOT a safe substitute either... It DOES refuse a junction that is already in place when the walk starts -- CPython's shutil._rmtree_isdir rejects IO_REPARSE_TAG_MOUNT_POINT (measured: victim intact). But that classification is read from DirEntry.stat(follow_symlinks=False), which on Windows is served from the PARENT directory's scandir cache and is never refreshed: measured, a DirEntry for a path that has since become a junction still reports st_reparse_tag == 0, and _rmtree_isdir returns True for it. So a live process that swaps an ALREADY-ENUMERATED sibling for a junction is followed -- measured 3/3 victims destroyed against the last entry of a large directory.
claims.why: The claim is about shutil.rmtree's behavior and is not verifiable from this chunk; it is a measured claim from the author and does not reference code in this chunk.

claims.text: This module therefore owns the delete, via _remove_tree_no_follow, whose invariant is that every path handed to a syscall that RESOLVES it -- os.scandir, os.rmdir, os.unlink, os.chmod, all four of them -- is re-classified with a FRESH lstat immediately beforehand; git worktree prune then deregisters.
claims.why: _remove_tree_no_follow is not defined in this chunk; the invariant cannot be checked here.

claims.text: That narrows the window to a few microseconds. It does not close it -- see the 'WHAT IS STILL NOT CLOSED' note on that function.
claims.why: Refers to a note on _remove_tree_no_follow, which is not in this chunk.

claims.text: Path hygiene cannot see an attack that uses no path trickery at all: the candidate os.renames the primary checkout INTO its own worktree, and every check then passes honestly, because what the walker finds is a real directory in a place it really is entitled to delete (measured, 3/3, whole checkout gone, cleanup returned success). What exists against it is one mitigation, not a fix -- see GitWorktreeManager._refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved.
claims.why: _refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved is not defined in this chunk; the claim about the mitigation cannot be verified.

claims.text: That mitigation is an IDENTITY check, and an earlier version of this paragraph said it 'knows the identity of exactly ONE directory'. That was wrong twice over. It was wrong about the SCOPE -- it now records the no-follow identity of the checkout AND of every directory the checkout is reached through, because the same attack one component higher (move the checkout's PARENT in, junction the parent's name) went straight past a leaf-only check: measured, 40/40 work files destroyed.
claims.why: The claim describes behavior of _refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved, which is not in this chunk.

claims.text: And it was wrong about the STRENGTH: what it knows is not an identity it cannot be lied to about. It read that identity with os.stat, which FOLLOWS a reparse point, so the answer came back THROUGH the attacker's own junction and matched. It reads os.lstat now. The honest statement is: it knows the no-follow identity of the checkout's chain as of the moment this manager was constructed, and forging one of those identities requires an object that does not exist yet to be handed an inode number that a live object still holds.
claims.why: The claim that os.lstat is used for identity is supported by _path_identity, which explicitly uses os.lstat and returns (st_dev, st_ino). The claim about the manager's identity check is uncheckable, but the statement about lstat being no-follow is kept.

claims.text: Refusals RAISE. A silently skipped cleanup leaks worktrees; a silently followed one deletes a repository. Both are loud.
claims.why: The exception classes WorktreeContainmentError and WorktreeRemovalRace are defined in this chunk, and the docstrings for those classes state that refusals raise. The existence of these exceptions supports the claim.

claims.text: Worktrees must live OUTSIDE the primary checkout so they never pollute git status or whole-repo snapshot attribution.
claims.why: The claim is a design intent; the code computes a path outside the repo, but the actual placement relative to the checkout is not verifiable without seeing the caller.

claims.text: Placement, in order: 1. DAEDALUS_WORKTREE_ROOT env override (still namespaced per repo). 2. %LOCALAPPDATA%/daedalus/worktrees. 3. tempfile.gettempdir()/daedalus/worktrees when LOCALAPPDATA is unset.
claims.why: The code checks DAEDALUS_WORKTREE_ROOT first, then LOCALAPPDATA, then tempfile.gettempdir(), and appends 'daedalus/worktrees' in the fallback cases. It also namespaces per repo with a digest.

claims.text: Each repo gets its own subdirectory keyed by a short digest of the resolved repo path so distinct checkouts never collide.
claims.why: The code computes a sha256 digest of str(repo_path) and truncates to 12 hex chars, then uses it as a subdirectory name.

claims.text: os.path.normpath collapses .. textually; unlike resolve() it cannot be redirected by a symlink, which is exactly the property needed before a containment decision.
claims.why: The implementation uses os.path.normpath and os.path.abspath, neither of which follows symlinks.

claims.text: Comparison form: case-folded on Windows, normalised everywhere.
claims.why: The implementation uses os.path.normcase (which case-folds on Windows) and os.path.normpath.

claims.text: True if child is parent or lies under it, lexically.
claims.why: The implementation compares normalized keys and checks prefix with os.sep and os.altsep.

claims.text: True for a symlink OR a Windows directory junction / mount point.
claims.why: The implementation checks S_ISLNK, os.path.islink, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_REPARSE_POINT, and st_reparse_tag.

claims.text: os.path.islink is NOT sufficient on Windows: a junction created with mklink /J has reparse tag IO_REPARSE_TAG_MOUNT_POINT, not ...SYMLINK, so islink returns False for it (measured on this machine). The FILE_ATTRIBUTE_REPARSE_POINT bit on lstat catches every reparse kind, including tags that do not exist yet.
claims.why: The implementation checks FILE_ATTRIBUTE_REPARSE_POINT and st_reparse_tag in addition to islink, which would catch junctions. The claim about islink not seeing junctions is consistent with Windows behavior.

claims.text: THE FIRST LINE IS THE ONLY ONE THAT EXISTS OFF WINDOWS... st_file_attributes and st_reparse_tag are not members of a stat_result on Linux/macOS at all, so on those platforms both getattr calls yield the default and deleting the S_ISLNK/islink line turns this whole function into return False -- every symlink followed, every guard in this file silently open. That mutation SURVIVED the suite until 2026-07-28; it is killed now by test_reparse_detection_off_windows_rests_on_the_symlink_branch, which simulates the POSIX stat SHAPE rather than skipping off Windows.
claims.why: The implementation uses getattr with defaults for st_file_attributes and st_reparse_tag, so on POSIX they default to 0 and the function relies on S_ISLNK/islink. The claim about the test is uncheckable, but the code behavior matches the described mutation risk.

claims.text: (st_dev, st_ino) for path ITSELF, or None if it is not there. NO-FOLLOW, and that is the whole point. It reads os.lstat, not os.stat.
claims.why: The implementation uses os.lstat and returns (st_dev, st_ino) or None on OSError/ValueError.

claims.text: An earlier version used os.stat, which FOLLOWS a reparse point, and that made the identity FORGEABLE by the one primitive this module exists to defend against -- measured on this box, against the manager's own repo_path: ... So a candidate that renamed the checkout aside and hung a mklink /J junction on its name was answering the 'is the checkout still the directory I was created for?' question THROUGH its own decoy. Measured end to end before this was changed: 40/40 tracked work files, SENTINEL.txt and .git destroyed, with the containment layer never refusing (the RuntimeError that came back was git worktree prune noticing afterwards that the repository was gone).
claims.why: The measured claims are about historical behavior and not verifiable from this chunk. The current code uses lstat, which is consistent with the claim that it now uses lstat.

claims.text: Measured on this box (Windows 11, CPython 3.10.11): lstat populates both fields for a DIRECTORY, os.rename PRESERVES them (same NTFS record under a new name -- so a renamed directory keeps its record and a fresh object cannot be handed that record while the renamed one still holds it), and a fresh directory OR JUNCTION created at the vacated name gets a different st_ino. So this distinguishes 'the same directory, still there' from 'moved away', from 'replaced by something wearing its name', and now from 'replaced by a link TO ITSELF wearing its name' -- none of which path text can.
claims.why: These are empirical claims about NTFS behavior, not verifiable from code in this chunk.

claims.text: st_ino is 0 on filesystems that do not expose one (FAT, some network mounts). Callers must treat a zero st_ino as NO identity rather than as a comparable value; see GitWorktreeManager._refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved, which is why that method also has a check that does not depend on inodes.
claims.why: The code returns (st_dev, st_ino) which could be (0,0) on such filesystems; the docstring's warning is consistent with the return type. The referenced method is not in this chunk.

claims.text: NOTE ON ALL FOUR PRIMITIVES BELOW. os.chmod, os.unlink and os.rmdir resolve their path ARGUMENT through a reparse point in any intermediate component, exactly as os.scandir does. (What they do NOT do is follow a reparse point that is the FINAL component -- rmdir removes the junction, unlink removes the link.) So none of them is safe on the strength of a check that happened earlier: every caller here re-verifies the whole chain immediately before calling them. An earlier version believed os.scandir was the only follower, and the rmdir drain that belief licensed was measured deleting 3000 directories inside a stand-in primary
claims.where: Comment before the removal section, lines 178-186
claims.why: The claim about the primitives resolving intermediate reparse points is consistent with Python semantics. The claim about callers re-verifying is uncheckable because the callers are not in this chunk, but the comment itself is a claim about them.

observations.what: The module docstring makes extensive claims about measured behavior on Windows and about the safety of _remove_tree_no_follow, but that function is not in this chunk. Downstream readers may rely on claims that cannot be verified from this chunk alone.

The no-follow containment relies on the correctness of _is_reparse_point and _path_identity. Any subtle platform difference (e.g., st_ino=0, missing st_file_attributes) could weaken the guard. The docstrings acknowledge some of these, but the code itself is not resilient against all edge cases.

The comment about the four primitives (os.chmod, os.unlink, os.rmdir, os.scandir) is truncated mid-sentence, but the claim about re-verifying the chain before each call is a promise about code not present in this chunk.
